research_question: What is the effect of testosterone pretreatment compared with placebo or no treatment on live birth or ongoing pregnancy in women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (IVF/ICSI)?
outcome_description: Live birth or ongoing pregnancy rate per randomised woman (live birth prioritised; ongoing pregnancy used when live birth is not reported)
positive_direction: A positive effect indicates higher odds of live birth or ongoing pregnancy favoring testosterone pretreatment compared with control
search_queries: testosterone pretreatment IVF trial live birth
transdermal testosterone ovarian stimulation randomized controlled trial
testosterone pretreatment poor responders ongoing pregnancy
inclusion_criteria: Randomised or controlled clinical trials evaluating testosterone pretreatment (e.g. transdermal gel or patch) prior to ovarian stimulation for IVF or ICSI
Comparisons of testosterone pretreatment against placebo or no pretreatment
Reporting live birth or ongoing pregnancy outcomes among women undergoing assisted reproduction
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative reviews, editorials, comments, and animal/in vitro studies)

No comparison between testosterone pretreatment and placebo or no treatment (e.g. studies using DHEA, other active interventions, or comparing different doses of testosterone without an untreated/placebo control)
No quantitative data reported on live birth or ongoing pregnancy per woman randomised
Completely unrelated to assisted reproductive technology (IVF/ICSI) or ovarian stimulation
moderators_to_extract: Testosterone formulation and route (e.g. transdermal gel vs patch)
Duration of testosterone pretreatment (e.g. <3 weeks vs >=3 weeks)
Control condition type (placebo vs no treatment)
Patient population characteristics (e.g. Bologna criteria poor responders vs general poor ovarian responders)
effect_size_note: Live birth or ongoing pregnancy analysed as odds ratios (OR). Where trials have multiple testosterone duration arms, the control group sample size is divided equally among comparisons to avoid unit-of-analysis error.
